posts.name: Jacek Czarnecki
posts.cooked:
It has been a year since I was just about to leave my job as the Global Legal Counsel at the Maker Foundation. Back then, I was very concerned about how MakerDAO would handle legal and regulatory topics moving forward. A month before my departure, in June 2021, I published a forum post about what I considered the regulatory topics of most importance.

That’s one of my main thoughts and messages to the community back then:

Mapping out policy challenges and opportunities for Maker

To put it simply, it is not enough to survive and avoid regulatory scrutiny. To grow and outcompete traditional finance, Maker will need sophisticated regulatory thinking embedded in its overall strategy.

Unfortunately, not much has happened since then. Regulatory thinking at MakerDAO is driven almost purely by news headlines, and the recent drama on discord around Tornado Cash sanctions is just an example. MakerDAO is reactive, underinformed, sometimes ignorant, and generally susceptible to superficial analyses. Rare counterexamples like SES legal research do not change the overall picture.

Are we seriously thinking about triggering some tectonic shifts in the economic structure of Dai and the Maker Protocol based on hearsay legal views?

Don’t worry; I didn’t come here to rant only. I wanted to present my perspective on some legal topics relevant to the current discussions. These are just my (quickly written) thoughts and not legal advice to anyone. It is also not an exclusive list (far from it).

Disclaimer: I do not represent anyone and anyone’s interests but just myself. I own MKR, but I appreciate my reputation and integrity more than my bags. Accordingly, I would like to see Maker continuing to be a respected, invincible, invulnerable, world-changing project more than any financial gains. Also, I don’t have anything against anons, but the invasion of anon accounts here has become unbearable, so I may decide not to engage in discussion with them.

Here are the relevant topics:

1. Dai regulation

Tl;dr any asset which pegs to fiat currency will be strictly regulated. Any issuer of such stablecoins will be regulated and licensed. Dai and Maker will be outlawed if they don’t follow the requirements. These regulations will be very difficult to comply with without a centralized structure in place.

This is the most important topic and yet the most overlooked one.

Stablecoin regulations are being cooked all around the globe. In some cases (EU), they are actually ready.

Many follow the thinking pattern, "when there is something certain, we will deal with that.” That fallacy inevitably leads to panic when something finally happens; see Tornado Cash and sanctions. It is sure what is going to happen.

Until 2020, one of the strategies I was pursuing in the Foundation was trying to “fly under the radar” and allow the policymakers to regulate centralized stablecoins while not sticking our neck out too much.

I dropped this approach after I was invited to a closed meeting of the Financial Stability Board, which consists of senior central bankers and regulators and coordinates global financial regulation. I came out from meetings and dinner with these folks, realizing they would want to have a global, all-encompassing, strict regulatory regime for any stablecoins.

That was 2.5 years ago. In the meantime, the FSB issued its report confirming the approach, and individual countries started implementing their regimes largely based on FSB’s recommendations.

One of the central premises of the stablecoin regulation, as implemented almost everywhere, is that it usually defines stablecoins as assets that in any form peg to a fiat currency. The exact nature of the peg does not matter. Especially after the UST collapse, one should not expect regulatory differentiation between centralized and decentralized stablecoins. In some places like the US, the debate is ongoing, but please be realistic about it.

Long story short, recently Nikolai and Rune explained how the USD peg inevitably leads to the dependence on USD-denominated assets. The same applies on the regulatory front: a fiat currency peg will soon trigger rigid regulations. One difference is that it’s not only about the US regulations (a peg to USD will still trigger the EU regulations, for instance).

Maker is enjoying the last months of the unregulated stablecoin wild west, but these times will be essentially over in 2023-24. I am not arguing either way, but Maker should either maintain the fiat currency peg and prepare for complex and centralizing regulations (perhaps impossible to comply with in some cases) or work out an alternative.

2. RWA

Tl;dr RWAs will bring regulatory troubles and costs on Maker.

I’ve been involved in RWAs since the early days. In 2017, just before joining Maker later that year, I was part of a German startup that was tokenizing equity. I was one of the persons working on RWAs in the Foundation when the topic first seriously emerged in 2018. In 2020-21, I led a side project that built a solution for decentralized security token trading and received the EU law green light from a regulator.

I don’t believe in RWAs in Maker. More specifically, I believe in small-scale diversification of collateral (let’s say <5%) and RWA experimentation. However, counting on RWA as the main bet and a cure for all Maker’s problems, the primary collateral source, and the source of decentralization (by that definition, almost any bank would be decentralized) was a misconception a few years ago, and it still is a misconception in 2022.

The main reasons are that RWAs erode decentralization (which is not appreciated by the users until it is; see TC and Genesis cases) and, even more importantly, that in the current form, they remove the transparency, hence stripping away the critical competitive advantages of Maker. Do we really want to see news articles about “what’s actually backing Dai and what’s in the newest reserve report” like the ones about Tether or USDC?

That’s not my point here, though. I want to clarify that the legal topics around RWAs are not limited to structuring the deals, which proves difficult enough by the way. Focus on RWAs will inevitably lead to regulatory burdens and troubles, particularly difficult to comply with by a DAO. This is shadow banking business under a pirate flag. Even if we finally sort out all the current issues in 1-2-3 years, the costs to comply with financial regulations will be enormous.

3. Sanctions and AML/KYC

Tl;dr do not enter panic mode over TC. Focus on solving the fundamental problems I mention in this post.

Let me keep this one short as there are a lot of discussions elsewhere—just two thoughts.

OFAC designation of Tornado Cash was directly related to its use in cybercrime. It’s another chapter in the ongoing war against mixers and anonymity-enhancing solutions in general. The Maker Protocol does not have much to do with these. I do not think a similar thing happening to Maker’s smart contracts is probable.

That said, of course, USDC freezing/blocking is a risk. This risk is, however, associated with the inherent censorship risks of RWAs rather than a direct sanctions risk for Maker. This risk is not new and is just one of many other ones (e.g., counterparty risk). This risk should be accounted for and mitigated. For example, Maker is the largest USDC user (3.5 billion USDC) and should not be treated at par with a random 10k USDC holder and Tornado Cash user.

There is, however, a real risk associated with the development of AML/KYC regulation. We will see further attacks on self-hosted wallets and forcing KYC everywhere. Maker should double down on its public policy and lobbying efforts in this area.

4. Decentralization / DeFi regulation

I will keep this one even shorter to not make this post totally indigestible, but I can elaborate later if needed.

Ultimately, decentralization is and will be our strongest moat against regulatory risks. It is easy to downplay the inefficiencies it brings, but it is of great protective value, not to mention other benefits. We should treat it with care. The fact that regulators are targeting decentralized protocols like Tornado Cash should not make us think differently—this is the only thing that gives TC a chance to survive. The same thing applies to other decentralized protocols, including Maker.

These are my quick thoughts. Happy to discuss.

posts.cooked:
Thank you for prompting this discussion here. I would add a few issues for consideration on this thread.

Disclaimer - these are a rough outline of concerns that shouldn’t be taken as advice. You should discuss any legal questions you have about the MakerDAO ecosystem or any other legal issues with your counsel. Most of my commentary is also from a US perspective, I hope others can weigh in on these and similar concerns from an international perspective (keeping in mind that the US does have a lot of extra-territorial regulatory influence).

DAO Entity Status

There is an underlying assumption by the community at large that the DAO has no legal entity status. This assumption is untested, and there is activity from regulators that suggests it might be wrong. Most notably is the SEC’s Report and Recommendation on the DAO: https://www.sec.gov/litigation/investreport/34-81207.pdf

Therein, the SEC asserts that the DAO is an “unincorporated organization” and that “[t]he DAO was ‘responsible for the success or failure of the enterprise,’ and accordingly, was the entity about which investors needed information material to their investment decision.” Id. at 16. So at least the SEC believes that DAOs are (or can be) legal entities subject to US securities law. We have also seen private parties bring litigation against DAOs. See, e.g., Sarcuni et al v. bZx DAO et al., Case No. 3:22-cv-618-LAB-DEB (Complaint) (“bZx protocol purports to be a so-called DAO, or decentralized autonomous organization, that lacks any legal formalities or recognition. There is another phrase in American law for that kind of arrangement: general partnership. That means each of the partners is jointly and severally liable to the Plaintiffs and must make good on the full amount of its debts.”) (emphasis in original). Likewise, we have even seen MakerDAO itself threatened with a patent infringement lawsuit: Infringement of TRS's U.S. Patent No. 10,025,797 by MakerDao

NB: I am not commenting on the merits of these cases, just that the concern is one that has to be taken seriously.

If an entity does exist, additional questions include what kind of entity (state unincorporated association? General partnership? Something else?), who the members are (all token holders? All forum members? Core Unit Facilitators? Delegates? Shadow Delegates? Folks that voted their tokens?) , what obligations DAO members have to eachother, what where the entity is subject to jurisdiction, what taxes does it (and it’s members) owe?

Securities Treatment of MakerDAO Related Digital Assets

Another key topic is what legal kind of assets are related to and issued by the MakerDAO protocol. The fight is typically framed as a question of whether particular assets are “commodities” or “securities.” At a high level, lots of crypto enthusiasts want tokens to be considered “commodities” which would be regulated by the CFTC; they have authority over, but (with some exceptions, especially regarding fraud) don’t restrict “spot” trading of commodities. Securities, on the other hand, are subject to a lot of restrictions on issuance, registration, sale, etc. by the SEC. This is in part why RWA transactions have to involve a broker/dealer like Genesis.

This determination has obvious implications for MKR, and Dai tokens, but this can also have potential implications for CDP’s, Vaults, or anything else that is tokenized. And not all tokens will necessarily be treated the same way.

Again, the Report on the DAO is one of the best official sources explaining the position of the SEC on this. See also https://www.sec.gov/corpfin/framework-investment-contract-analysis-digital-assets. The Hinman Speech is a good overview for non-lawyers on some of the key concepts, but the SEC is now trying to disclaim this in the Ripple litigation. https://www.sec.gov/news/speech/speech-hinman-061418. All of these sources reference the Howey test articulated in a 1946 Supreme Court case. SEC v. WJ Howey Co., 328 US 293 - Supreme Court 1946 - Google Scholar. The BlockFi case has also highlighted the importance of the Reves test. https://www.sec.gov/litigation/admin/2022/33-11029.pdf

Although they’ve gotten less attention, other important issues include:

  • Securitization of digital assets–if you pledge digital assets to secure a loan, then transfer them without permission, lender may (or may not) be able to go after the third-party transferee to reclaim them, depending on state law.
  • Bankruptcy–lately, this has been an issue for CeFi exchanges, with users frustrated that they may be treated as unsecured creditors rather than secured creditors with a claim on their crypto deposits. But this could also become an issue in DeFi; imagine if a vault holder declares bankruptcy–are keepers that move to liquidate their vault breaching the automatic stay? What if the USD peg breaks and Dai is undercollateralized and a user files an involuntary bankruptcy petition against MakerDAO; is there an obligation to institute an emergency freeze?
  • Money transmission–in addition to OFAC, FinCEN has fined a handful for prominent crypto firms for engaging in money transmission without a money transmitter license, or failing to keep KYC/AML records. There are also state regimes to consider.

–

Stepping back to your comments, I very much agree that we need long term and not reactionary thinking. I also want to see Maker continue to be a respected and important part of not only the DeFi ecosystem, but the world more broadly.

I have some skepticism of your analysis of the coming stablecoin regime. My read on proposes US regulation is not that anything pegged to a Fiat currency must comply with a forthcoming regulatory regime for stabelcoins. Rather, the Lumis-Gillibrand bill limits “Payment Stablecoin” digital assets “redeemable, on demand, on a one-to-one basis for instruments … defined as legal tender under section 5103…” which Dai, even considering the PSM, is not (USDC is not defined as legal tender). https://www.gillibrand.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Lummis-Gillibrand%20Responsible%20Financial%20Innovation%20Act%20[Final].pdf. We’re still waiting for the text of the Boozman-Staenow bill, but my secondhand understanding of discussions with staffers is that it would only capture redeemable stablecoins, and not algorithmic or collateralized stablecoins like Dai. Further, the Lumis-Gillibrand bill would likely push Dai towards being treated as a commodity (though the new regulatory framework for “ancillary assets” still does not perfectly fit the Maker Ecosystem). But these bills could also be bad for Maker if Treasury and the SEC decide that the passage of a regulatory framework for stablecoins means its open season to make life hell for any nonconforming coins.

I pretty much agree with the rest of the factual information you present, but I’m not sure I understand the conclusion you reach. You agree that trying to fly under the radar is not a viable strategy, but seem to be against anything that leads to engagement with regulators. I am not sure how this is a viable strategy. Maybe regulators can’t touch the protocol itself, but the IRS, SEC, Treasury, DOJ, and swath of state regulators (and I would assume European regulators) can make life hard for the users of the protocol.

I also think there is a third option between full regulator compliance and centralization vs. outright defiance. The SEC wants to make law that will serve them well, and to do that, they are likely to litigate against underfinanced, unsympathetic defendants, that judges won’t hesitate to bring the hammer down on. But web3 entities with a sheen of legitimacy, that don’t hurt consumers, are less likely to be regulatory targets. It reminds me of a joke:

a couple guys are walking in the forest and see a vicious bear that starts heading towards them. The first guy immediately takes a knee and starts tightening his shoelaces. The second guy shouts, “you’re crazy! You’ll never outrun the bear!”
The first guy replies: “I don’t have to outrun the bear, I just have to outrun you.”

A bunch of DeFi projects are eventually going to fall, as regulation drives away capital. To not get caught and become one of these projects, the Maker community should proactively respond to regulators, dismantling their legal case before they can bring it.

The harder question for me to answer is “how does the community do that.” I don’t have a fully fleshed out idea. And I don’t think the answer can or should be “relaunch with a blacklist.” But it might involve creating some sort of entities similar to what RWF has been doing to be the point of contact for regulated entities and individuals concerned about regulation. And in the long term, Dai needs to grow broad enough in adoption that it would be so disruptive to shut it down as to be politically infeasible.

0xbocaJ:

A bunch of DeFi projects are eventually going to fall, as regulation drives away capital. To not get caught and become one of these projects, the Maker community should proactively respond to regulators, dismantling their legal case before they can bring it.

Good post with some nice detail and investigation @0xbocaJ

I disagree with the above. While I think engagement with regulators should be undertaken as a show of good faith, I think engagement to “dismantle their legal case before they can bring it” isn’t a viable strategy. In fact engaging in this fashion will likely put the individual or entity right smack in the line of litigation.

Also as others have commented @GFXlabs the likely approach here to deal with a DAO is to treat DAO’s as general partnerships and basically go after the weakest links.

I also think the treatment of the issuance of the DAOs (various Tokens they issue) vs. the DAOs themselves creates a greater surface area for regulatory litigation.

There are many deep issues to consider here. One of them is this idea a lot of people have that Maker and DAI be committed to being decentralized and this somehow saves everything from being attacked. I dispute this assertion and would counter that as @GFXlabs has suggested Maker rapidly figure out the most favorable jurisdiction to home in and then work out all the details of international regulatory compliance ‘from that jurisdiction’. Anything short of doing this basically opens the DAO up to the application of ALL regulatory laws, across ALL jurisdictions on each and every party in said jurisdiction.

Short of legislators coming around to an idea that a network in effect becomes its own jurisdiction (like it’s own nation state) or some similar special treatment of blockchain networks (both of these treatments highly unlikely to come to pass imo) in absence of a jurisdiction and a legal entity to go with it regulators and legislators are likely to treat DAOs and associated digital assets as they do all other threats to their sovereignty and citizenry.

Which is why I have been suggesting that DeFI projects organize and fund a collective to both propose a global legal framework for the space, and then educate and lobby regulators to implement some form of proposed organizational/leal model internationally. Anything short of this will leave the space constantly battling on one or more fronts.
